plan.topic: Food noise on tirzepatide: why cravings can go quiet, and why Halloween candy may feel different (Psychiatric Times, Oct 28, 2026)
plan.angle: 13:00 Halloween Short, 170 words or fewer. Open with: 'Halloween candy not calling your name on tirzepatide? There may be biology behind that.' Use a peer-reviewed review for how GLP-1 signals act on the brain's appetite and reward areas, labelling animal findings 'in mice' or 'in rats' and human findings 'in people'. Honest line: 'One case report, in a single person, found tirzepatide quieted craving-linked brain activity, but it came back after about five months (Nature Medicine, 2025). That's early research, not proof.' Call it 'a case report in one person', never a study. Habits: eat slowly, stop when comfortably full, and enjoy a treat without guilt. GI line: very sweet or greasy treats may sit less well. No restriction, 'cure' or binge-eating treatment language. Add 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. Loop ending. Don't cite Psychiatric Times.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide and Food Noise: Why Halloween Candy Feels Different #shorts
plan.why: 'Food noise' is one of the most searched GLP-1 phrases, and Halloween is 2 days away. This replaces the usual 13:00 head-to-head because no fresh tirzepatide trial is available, and the retatrutide trial is already used by S3 under the one-trial-per-week rule. | fact-check: I couldn't find the cited Psychiatric Times article from Oct 28, 2026, so don't cite it. The 'small, early tirzepatide study' is really a single-patient case report. Shivacharan et al., Nature Medicine, Nov 17, 2025 (Penn Medicine), recorded brain activity through implanted electrodes in 4 trial participants, but the tirzepatide finding comes from 1 woman. Her craving-linked reward-centre (nucleus accumbens) activity and food preoccupation went quiet at her full dose, then came back after about 5 months. Calling it a 'study' with a group size would overstate it. The authors warn the drugs aren't a fix for binge eating 'in their current form', so make no binge-eating treatment claims. No trial has tested Halloween candy specifically, so frame that part as 'may'. Brain-reward mechanism findings are mostly from animals; label them 'in mice' or 'in rats'.

factcheck.summary: The science holds up and the Short is safe. Six of the seven sources were checked; Müller 2019 (src1) wasn't opened. Dickson 2012: exendin-4 was injected into the VTA and nucleus accumbens of rats and reduced the reward from sucrose and chocolate. Van Bloemendaal 2014: 48 obese people with type 2 diabetes, obese people without diabetes and lean people; IV exenatide reduced brain responses to food pictures in the obese groups. Choi et al., Nature Medicine, 17 Nov 2025: one 60-year-old woman with severe obesity and loss-of-control eating, who had electrodes in her nucleus accumbens for a brain-stimulation trial and was on tirzepatide for type 2 diabetes. Her craving-linked signal went quiet, then came back after about 5 months. The CUH leaflet supports eating slowly, stopping when full and choosing low-fat foods when nauseous. The script handles the evidence well: animal first, then human, then a single person, and it says "early research, not proof". It is about 169 words, the safety lines are present and there's no dosing or medication-change advice. Four minor fixes: (1) s6 puts a source tag on our own "without guilt" tip; (2) s4 says "one dose" when it was an IV infusion; (3) s5 leaves out that the patient was on tirzepatide for type 2 diabetes and that the brain recording came from implanted electrodes; (4) s7's fatty-food advice is tagged to the NHS page, which doesn't say it.

issues.claim: Eat slowly, stop when comfortably full, and enjoy a treat without guilt. (source_ids: src7)
issues.problem: The CUH leaflet supports "eat slowly" and "stop when you are feeling full". "Enjoy a treat without guilt" is our own tip, and the rules say our own tips get no source tag. If a src7 tag is shown on screen, it covers a line the source didn't write.
issues.fix: Keep the narration. If the src7 tag is shown, put it only on "Eat slowly" and "Stop when comfortably full". Show no tag on "Enjoy a treat without guilt".

issues.claim: In people with obesity, one dose of exenatide, another GLP-one drug, dampened brain-scan responses to food pictures.
issues.problem: Van Bloemendaal 2014 gave exenatide as a single IV infusion during a clamp in the lab. That isn't the weekly injection viewers use, and "one dose" blurs the difference. The on-screen item should also show the scope.
issues.fix: Narration: "In people with obesity, a single IV infusion of exenatide, another GLP-one drug, dampened brain-scan responses to food pictures." On-screen item 2: "People with obesity (n=48 incl. lean): one IV exenatide infusion, brain scans of food pictures".

issues.claim: One case report, in a single person with severe obesity and loss-of-control eating, found tirzepatide quieted craving-linked brain activity, but it came back after about five months.
issues.problem: This is accurate but leaves out context that limits how far it applies. She was on tirzepatide for type 2 diabetes, and her brain activity was recorded through electrodes implanted for a brain-stimulation trial. It's also an observation in one person, not a test, so "found tirzepatide quieted" sounds a bit more causal than the evidence allows.
issues.fix: Narration: "Here's the catch. In one person with severe obesity, loss-of-control eating and type 2 diabetes, implanted brain electrodes showed craving-linked activity going quiet on tirzepatide, then returning after about five months. That's early research, not proof." (Same word count, give or take 3 words.) stat_label: "1 person with type 2 diabetes and loss-of-control eating: craving signal returned after ~5 months".

issues.claim: Rich, fatty treats may sit less well, especially if you feel queasy. (source_ids incl. src6)
issues.problem: The NHS tirzepatide page lists nausea, vomiting, constipation and diarrhoea, but gives no advice about fatty food. That advice comes from the CUH leaflet ("eat bland, low-fat foods" when nauseous). The SURMOUNT-1 paper supports "mostly mild to moderate".
issues.fix: Tag "Rich, fatty treats may sit less well" to src7 only. Tag the side-effect list to src5 and src6, and "mostly mild to moderate" to src5.
